source.title: Leveraging Flatness to Improve Information-Theoretic Generalization Bounds for SGD
source.authors: Ze Peng; Jian Zhang; Yi-Sen Wang; Lei Qi; Ying-Huan Shi; Yang Gao

record.file_problem: Text contains the full paper and appendices; no apparent truncation or document mismatch.
record.tranche_reason: It reports generalization measurements while varying batch size and network width, extending those comparisons to ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 and a two-layer MLP on MNIST. It does not test the claim’s specified original model recipes.
record.gate_note: The paper’s own experiments report generalization gaps under varied batch size and width. Other related discussion of flatness and prior results is not itself a row unless the paper reports its own outcome. Figure-only values are recorded without reconstructing numbers.
record.test_reason: The experiments measure capped cross-entropy generalization gaps, defined as population loss minus training loss, rather than held-out classification error or held-out loss itself. A smaller gap does not establish better held-out performance when training losses can differ. The width experiments also do not establish zero training error or locate the interpolation threshold. Consequently, these results do not directly test V2 or V5, and no other version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that their omniscient-trajectory bound better exploits Hessian flatness, tracks measured generalization-gap trends, and is numerically tighter. They also derive an O(1/sqrt(n)) minimax excess-risk bound for gradient descent on convex-Lipschitz-bounded problems. They acknowledge heavy reliance on population gradients and Hessians and an incorrectly directed learning-rate trend in the trajectory term.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates information-theoretic generalization bounds on trained networks; it does not use the original interventions or measurement recipes for the listed versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported generalization and bound tendencies vary with batch size and learning rate. The authors state that the trajectory term’s tendency with learning rate remains incorrect, while the batch-size tendency is corrected in their bound.

fits_no_version.finding: For ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10 under fixed 200-epoch training, the authors explicitly report that smaller batches produce smaller capped cross-entropy generalization gaps among retained runs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Smaller batches reduce the capped cross-entropy test–train gap in this training setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Width sweeps evaluate cross-entropy generalization gaps for ResNet-18 and a two-layer MLP, without establishing interpolation or reporting a readable directional result in the supplied figure text.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Network width can be studied as a determinant of cross-entropy generalization gaps independently of post-interpolation test-error claims.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed bound tracks several measured gap trends more closely and is numerically tighter than the compared information-theoretic bounds; its interpretation emphasizes alignment between output-weight covariance and Hessian flatness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizing an omniscient auxiliary trajectory can improve information-theoretic bounds on cross-entropy generalization gaps.

record.problems: The width and batch-size trend values are shown in figures without exact numbers or uncertainty estimates in the text. Experiments use six independently trained models per hyperparameter and exclude records with final training accuracy below 95%. The paper states that test accuracy on CIFAR-10 is relatively low because each model uses one-sixth of the training set. The authors identify reliance on population gradients and Hessians as a major limitation.
record.rows_left_out: No additional eligible results omitted. Other figure panels vary learning rate, training-data usage, label-noise level, depth, weight decay, and weight scaling, but the text does not provide a specific directional result for the underlying generalization measurement for each of these conditions; the cited summary statements concern the bound’s ability to capture trends.

untested.parts: Near-perfect fitting of fixed random labels together with natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label held-out accuracy.
Whether widening beyond the width needed for zero training error continues to lower test error.
Matched convolutional versus fully connected classification performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance itself under fixed epoch budgets, and whether recipe adaptations remove those effects.

Magnitude-scaled perturbation tolerance and its ranking of generalization gaps against norm- and margin-based measures. Hessian-based bounds and covariance alignment do not measure this specified sharpness construct.
Retraining after removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is not an original source for any listed version. Its main purpose is bound evaluation, but its empirical gap measurements are its own results. Their mismatch with the versions' outcome measures precludes verdicts; it does not constitute evidence against those versions.

versions.untested_parts: Does not report fitting fixed random labels and comparing held-out accuracy with natural-label training.

Width is varied in the paper’s own experiments, but the result is figure-only and the text does not state the direction of the test-error change; the tested models and training setup also differ from the specified one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected image classifiers for generalization.
No adaptive optimizer versus SGD generalization comparison.
Tests batch-size variation on ResNet-18/CIFAR-10, but not the stated language-model settings or the full set of recipe adaptations in this version.
Does not test magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness against the specified norm- and margin-based measures.
Does not remove memorized examples and measure the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.operation_detail: Varied batch size while holding the other base hyperparameters fixed, except in the learning-rate/batch-size grid experiments.

conditions.value: varied; values not stated in text

rows.note: Authors state that actual generalization error decreases as batch size decreases. Six independent models were trained at each hyperparameter; models with final training accuracy below 95% were excluded.
rows.check: The stated batch-size trend concerns the capped cross-entropy test–train gap, not the held-out performance named by V5. The trend itself is explicitly reported, but cannot establish V5 without corresponding training or held-out losses. Figure 3 varies learning rate and batch size jointly in a grid; batch-size comparisons must hold learning rate fixed. Six models use disjoint training subsets and a shared initialization, and runs below 95% training accuracy are excluded. The explicit directional statement occurs in the introduction discussing Figure 1.

rows.subject: ResNet-18
rows.size_stated: channel scaling factor varied; exact values not stated in text
rows.operation_detail: Varied width using channel scaling while other single-variation hyperparameters were held at the base setting.
rows.note: Figure 4 includes width variation, but the text does not state the direction of the measured generalization change.
rows.check: Figure 4 measures a capped cross-entropy generalization gap rather than test error. Neither the width needed for zero training error nor continued interpolation across widths is established; the inclusion criterion is only at least 95% training accuracy. The supplied figure text does not preserve a readable direction for the measured width trend.
